findings.reason: Both instances share 'Married-civ-spouse' as marital status. This feature is highly correlated with socioeconomic stability and often co-occurs with higher income, but in the context of the dataset, it is statistically significant due to structural biases in the data. However, 'Married-civ-spouse' is not directly predictive of income; instead, its association arises because many married individuals belong to populations with higher education and employment rates, which are proxy indicators of income. This co-occurrence may reflect a spurious correlation with the target class due to imbalanced labeling and demographic bias in the training data.

Both instances have 'Husband' as relationship status. This feature is semantically weak in predicting income, as 'Husband' status does not inherently imply income level. Instead, it often correlates with household structure and marital status, which are indirectly related to income through family responsibilities and cohabitation patterns. This could be a spurious signal due to data leakage—where the relationship status is correlated with demographic features (e.g., education, age, workclass) that are predictive of income. In a class-imbalanced dataset, such features may appear relevant due to overrepresentation in one class and thus mislead model prediction.
